# Design exploration

A design exploration is a dialog. **The user is the designer. You find and frame. The user
chooses.** A finding is not a licence to pick the fix.

The unit of work is one open question, with every answer drawn side by side at the same
geometry: a **sketch** on a product, or a **call** in a repository with the old setup. A variant wins
or loses only against the other variants of its question.

## The rules

1. **One open call at a time.** Take one question. Draw its variants. Stop.
2. **Put the variants in the call, then name your pick.** Two to four variants, drawn for
   real, side by side, labelled, with what each one costs. Your pick is a proposal. Never ask
   a yes/no question about content, and never ask the user what they want: deliver strong
   variants, and the user picks.
3. **Commit only when the user says commit.** A merge the user makes in Ethlete Studio counts as
   that word for the merged part: commit the part, not the open sketches.
4. **A clear rejection starts the next call.** Settle and record the rejected call, then draw
   the next focused question automatically, within the user's original scope. Stop only when the
   user asks to pause or end the exploration, or when their feedback leaves no grounded next
   question.
5. **Keep the answer short.** 120 words at most.

Confirm the step size once, at the start. Do not ask again at every stop. A task is not
finished while the user is still talking about it.

## What one stop looks like

- The question, in one sentence.
- The sketch (or call slug) to look at.
- The variants, labelled A, B, C, one line each.
- Your pick, one line on why.
- Nothing else. No next step, no second finding.

**Do not send a screenshot.** The user keeps the call open. Screenshot only for your own
check that a variant renders. In a repository with `et design`, take it with
`et design shot <layer>/<name> --states [--variants]`: one contact sheet of every state, and
every variant of the open sketch, with a label per cell; below each variant row, a diff row marks
the pixels that differ from the merged state in red, or says "no pixel change" (with ", but the markup differs" when only the markup changed, e.g. both sides miss the same content). It prints the PNG path last. `--scale 2` enlarges a small part; `--crop x,y,w,h` cuts each cell to that CSS-pixel box, to judge hairlines. `--interaction hover` forces an interaction on every cell. `--state a,b` draws only those states, to compare them side by side. With `--variants`, `--diff-props` compares each variant with the merged part drawn with the variant's state props, so changed props do not paint the diff red. It draws
undimmed, whatever Studio shows. Do not write a scratch script for batch shots.

If a second defect appears, add it to the open list and give it one line. Do not draw it.

## Where the variants are drawn

The exploration's plan file names the tool. Two shapes exist.

**A repository with a `.ethlete/design` folder** keeps one design system per **product**, and the
user reads and decides in Ethlete Studio. The tool is `et design`, from `@ethlete/cli`; run
`et design --help` for every command, `et design <command> [<subcommand>] --help` for one.

```
.ethlete/design/
  config.json                         the port and one `products` entry each
  <product>/<layer>/<part>/           layer: foundations, components, elements, pages
  <product>/flows/<name>.json         a flow: pages and their states joined by lines
  <product>/sketches/<layer>-<name>/  an open sketch: sketch.json and one folder per variant
  <product>/comments/<id>.json        a comment the user wrote in Studio
  calls/                              old calls: Legacy, read-only
```

Studio no longer takes new calls. **New work goes to a product, never to a new call**; do not run
`et design new`. Old calls stay in Studio's Legacy tab as reference for moving them into a
product. They take no picks and no new variants.

### Create a product

```bash
et design product new <name> [--base @ethlete/components|<path>] [--from-project <name>]
```

It writes the `config.json` entry and the empty layer folders. A product on `@ethlete/components`
takes the SDK as its base, so its parts start from the real components rendered with `ng()`.
Without a base it gets the presets phone (390x844) and desktop (1440x900). A product's own `presets`
replace its base's whole: a desktop-only app lists `desktop` alone and draws no phone state. `--from-project` copies
`styles`, `head`, `providers` and `themes` from an old project entry. Studio never writes
`config.json`; the command does.

Every frame loads the product's `foundations/tokens` stylesheet once, before the part's own
`styles`, so a part never imports the tokens and never adds them to its `styles`. A product's own
`foundations/tokens`, or a sketch of it, replaces the base's tokens in every frame. Never list a
`tokens.css` in config `styles`.

A part file default-exports its `definePart(...)` and may also export named helpers, such as a piece of its
markup: `import { studioMark } from '@system/foundations/logo'`. Import a piece from the part that draws it;
never copy its markup into another part. A piece that uses the part's classes needs its stylesheet too
(`@system/foundations/logo.css?inline`), or from the part's default export when the part sets
`definePart({ styles })`: every drawing of that part gets it, so `render` returns only extra styles. The layer
rules hold for these imports as well.

A component a host embeds exports its markup as such a helper, and a wrapper only its own frame needs, such as
padding that makes room for a focus ring, goes in `render` alone, never in that helper: the host places the
component itself and would inherit the wrapper's offset.

A product whose app uses Tailwind lists one stylesheet in config `styles` that imports the app's styles and
registers the drawing folders with `@source './'`. Sketches then use the app's utilities; plain CSS stays for what
utilities cannot express, such as camera geometry.

### Propose a change as a sketch

A change to a part, or a new part, is a **sketch**: the question is the part, the variants are the
answers. Variants are drawn at the same geometry, and one variant wins only against the others.

```bash
et design sketch new <layer>/<name> --variants a,b --by <model id> [--like <layer>/<name>] [--variant-note a=<text>]… [--product <p>]   # each variant starts as a copy of the part
et design sketch report <layer>/<name> --variant b --by <model id> "phone"         # tell Studio what you build now
et design sketch report <layer>/<name> --variant b --by <model id> --done         # you stopped drawing b; Studio shows its frames
et design sketch check [<layer>/<name>] [--fix]                                    # each variant laid over the product
et design sketch ready <layer>/<name> --by <model id>                              # now the user can pick
```

Variants are alternatives. A variant never stands for a state of another variant: a hidden or
collapsed mode of variant d is a further state of d, not a variant e. Before you draw a new control,
look for a control that already does the job (an active rail button that toggles its panel), and
draw that first.

A section of an app is a page under `pages/`, never a state of the shell. An element holds its
own chrome only. A sketch on an element adds no state whose difference is page content in a slot.

A variant mirrors the product layout and holds only the parts it changes. Draw two to four
variants, each with what it costs, and run `sketch check` before `ready`. A variant with problems
cannot be picked. A part in a variant keeps every state the part has in the product: `sketch check`
and `sketch ready` fail on a dropped state, and warn when two stylesheets of one part define the same class. Use `sketch list` to see the open ones.
`sketch check` also runs tsc over each variant with its `@shared/` and `@system/` imports, so never write a
tsconfig of your own. It warns of a variant stylesheet that restyles a class of `shared/`, and of a
variant file nothing imports. To delete a file of a part, delete it in the variant: a merge deletes the
product file the picked variant no longer holds.

Each variant's note, what it is and what it costs, goes in the `definePart({ note })` of its part file;
a merge keeps the picked variant's note. `sketch new --variant-note a=<text>`, once per variant, writes it.
`sketch new` and `sketch variant` write their files in the checkout's Prettier format; after an edit,
`sketch check --fix` formats the variants before it checks them. A sketch command
without `--product` takes the product that holds the sketch.

Start a new part from a close one with `--like`: `sketch new pages/inbox --like pages/system`
copies the product's `pages/system` into each variant, renamed to the target and without its
`madeBy`; `--like pages/system:b` copies variant b of the open sketch on it, with that sketch's
`shared/` folder.

Code the variants of one sketch have in common (sample data, a switch, a helper) goes in the
sketch's `shared/` folder, next to the variant folders, never into copies per variant. A part in a
variant imports it as `@shared/<path>`, and a shared file may import `@system/...` and
`@shared/...`. A part outside a sketch may not import `@shared/`. A variant that needs a shared file
changed holds its own copy at `<variant>/shared/<path>`; `@shared/<path>` finds that copy first, and a merge
of that variant takes it. On a merge, `shared/` moves into
the target's folder as `shared/` with its imports made relative; when no part imports it, it is
dropped. Only the target may import it: a merge refuses while another part of the picked variant
does, so move that code into the part. `sketch new` prints each file it puts in `shared/`, for example
the `shared/` folder of a merged page: edit it there, as part of the sketch, not in a variant copy.

```ts
// sketches/pages-flows/shared/flow-data.ts
export const flows = [{ name: 'Checkout', steps: 4 }];

// sketches/pages-flows/a/pages/flows/flows.ts
import { flows } from '@shared/flow-data';
```

An asset (a mark, logo, icon, picture or font) is one file in `.ethlete/design/<product>/assets/`,
never a copy inlined into parts. A part imports it as `@assets/<file>`: the default import is a URL
for `<img src>`; an SVG that must follow tokens (`currentColor`, `var(--accent)`) imports with
`?raw` and goes inline, for example `@assets/icons/<name>.svg?raw`. A stylesheet, the product's
`styles.css` or a part's, uses `url('@assets/<file>')`, for example in an `@font-face`. A foundation
part may wrap an asset in a named export. A product finds its base product's assets too. A sketch
variant adds or changes an asset in its own `<variant>/assets/` folder (`sketch new` and `sketch variant`
print it next to the part file), and a merge copies it into the product's. Size an inline SVG with
`svgAsset(mark, { size: 32 })` from `@design-system`, never by replacing its `width`/`height` as a
string; `class` and `attrs` (`{ 'aria-hidden': 'true' }`) set the rest of the root's attributes. `design check` fails an SVG asset with no root `<svg>` or without
`xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"` (an `<img src>` and an image viewer do not draw it). The part hash behind `design check` and "changed outside a sketch" counts the bytes of
the assets a part uses.

Every change to a merged part goes through a sketch, also a small one: new copy, sample data, an
added state. When there is nothing to choose, the sketch has one variant (`--variants a`), and the
user merges it or comments on it. Never edit a merged part directly, or the user cannot compare or
comment on the change in Studio. `design check` warns, and Studio marks the part "changed", when a
merged part changed outside a sketch; only a merged sketch on that part clears it.

A sketch on a foundations part such as `foundations/tokens` keeps the part's overview drawing: the
variant adds its token group as a state, or extends that group's state. It never replaces the
drawing with a demo scene, since the merge would drop every other group. A demo may be an extra state.

Name the variant you work on with `--variant`. Studio marks it as drawing, and hides its frames,
while the latest report names it. `sketch new`, `sketch variant` and each report record your
model id as an author of the variants they write, and `sketch ready` records it on every variant
that has no author yet. A merge adds the picked variant's authors to the `madeBy` the part file
already holds, and never removes it.

### Combine variants in a new round

Studio never combines variants. When the user asks for one in a comment ("solid like a, outline
like b"), draw it as a new variant in a new round:

```bash
et design sketch variant <layer>/<name> c --from a --by <model id> --round "Solid a, outline b" --note "r1 showed pill and square; the user wants a's solid with b's outline"
```

`--from` copies a variant into the new one, sets the sketch back to in progress and clears the
pick; it refuses while the decision is a discard (the user picks a variant first). Without `--round` the new variant joins the running round; with it, `--note` is required and
goes on the running round: what it showed and why its variants lost. Older variants stay pickable.
The command prints the notes of the previous round. Fix a round's title or note later with `sketch round <layer>/<name> <round> --title … --note … --by <model id>`; `sketch list` shows each sketch's rounds.
Letters continue across rounds (r1: a, b; r2: c, d). `sketch variant <layer>/<name> c,d --from a` adds
several variants at once; with `--round` they all start the new round. A new round answers the comments on the
`--from` variant and marks them "addressed in round" with the new round's key. A variant without `--round` fails while the sketch has open comments and lists them: a variant that answers a comment starts a new round. Draw the combined
variant and mark the sketch `ready` again. `sketch new --round <title> --note <text>` names
round 1 and sets its note; `--round` without `--note` fails. `sketch ready` refuses while the running round has no note; set it with `sketch round`.
`sketch ready` also shoots every state of every variant and of the product's part: when not one pixel differs
in any of them, it merges the sketch itself and logs it as an `auto` entry in the product's `accepted.json`
("No visible change in any state: merged automatically."). Any difference or failed shot leaves it `ready`.
A problem the product already had before the merge does not block it (the check prints it as a note); only a problem the merge adds does.
Run `sketch ready` again on a `ready` sketch to repeat the check and the auto merge.

### Your model id: `--by`

Every command that writes takes `--by <model id>` and fails without it: `sketch new`, `variant`, `report`,
`ready`, `rebase`, `merge`, `discard`, `inbox done` and `comment reply`. The id is the exact model
id as free text, for example `claude-opus-5-5`, `gpt-5.6-sol` or `gemini-3-argon`. Studio shows it
on the variant, the reply and the part, so the user sees which model made what.

**Never guess your id.** Use the one your prompt names. If your prompt names none and you do not
know your own exact id, ask the coordinator or the user before you write.

### The user decides, Studio merges

The user picks a variant, or discards the sketch, in Studio. **Studio merges on the user's click.
Never run `sketch merge` or `sketch discard` yourself, and never pick a variant.** Both mark
the open comments on the sketch's variants addressed: the user's click answers them. Comments on the
product's parts stay. If a part the variant replaces changed
in the product since the sketch was created, the merge refuses: bring each variant up to date, run
`et design sketch rebase <layer>/<name>`, and mark it `ready` again. `sketch preview <layer>/<name>
<variant>` lists the elements and pages a merge changes. The note on a part records why it has its
current shape. The user's reason is optional: with one, the merge sets the note from it; without
one, the part keeps the `note` the picked variant file holds, so write that note while you draw.

After the user approves a direct edit of a merged part (no sketch), run `et design accept <layer>/<name> --product <p> --by <model id> --note <why>` so `design check` stops warning `changed outside a sketch`. Never accept an edit the user did not approve.

### Read the inbox

The user comments on a state of a part in Studio, at a point, or on a sketch variant. The sketch of
an element also shows each page that uses it, with each variant swapped in: a comment there names
the page as its part and the element's sketch variant, so change the variant, not the page.

```bash
et design inbox [--json] [--product <p>]   # open comments and rebases, then what waits for the user
et design inbox done <id> --note <text> --by <model id>   # set the part note, mark the thread addressed
et design comment reply <id> --by <model id> <text> [--question]   # answer a comment thread (takes --product)
```

Read the inbox at the start of a session and after each sketch you mark `ready`. Answer a comment
by changing the sketch or the part, then `inbox done <id> --note "…"`. The note replaces the `note` of the part the comment was made on (for a sketch variant, the product's part), so write it to explain the whole shape of the part, and pass the old note unchanged when it still holds. `done` fails without `--note`; only the user withdraws a comment without one, in Studio. `done` also stores your `--by` where the comment sat: in the authors of the sketch variant, or in the `madeBy` of the part. A pick or discard decision is listed as waiting
for the user: Studio merges or discards on the user's click, so never run `sketch merge` after a pick.

A comment is a thread: the user and you both reply. When a comment is unclear, ask with
`comment reply --question` instead of guessing. The thread then moves to the "waiting for the user" group
(`waitingForUser` in `--json`) and returns to the inbox when the user answers. A thread there is
not work for you.

A thread has three states. **Open** waits for an answer. **Addressed** (`addressed`: who, when, why,
the round) means `inbox done`, a new round, a merge or a discard answered it: it leaves the inbox and
the check, Studio shows it with an "addressed" badge, and you may still `comment reply` on it to say
what you changed. A reply by the user opens it again. **Resolved** means the user closed it in Studio -
only the user resolves. The file stays so the user can look back at it; a reply or `done` on it fails.

Pass `--question` only when you cannot go on without the user's answer. Studio lists only those
threads under "Questions for you". A report of what you did is no question: reply without the
flag, and the thread shows as "answered" until the user withdraws it or replies.

### Draw a flow

A flow joins states of pages into a path the user reads left to right in Studio's Flows view.
It is `<product>/flows/<name>.json`; `position` and `label` are optional:

```json
{
  "frames": [{ "part": "pages/library", "state": "empty", "position": { "x": 0, "y": 0 } }],
  "lines": [
    {
      "from": { "part": "pages/library", "state": "empty" },
      "to": { "part": "pages/film-detail", "state": "default" },
      "label": "user adds a film"
    }
  ]
}
```

Every flow line is labelled, and the element the label names is visible in the frame before it: a line
labelled "user clicks 'Log in'" starts from a frame that shows a "Log in" button. A line that names
nothing the reader can see, or a label for a control the page lacks, is a defect.

A line may join two states of one page. A frame may name a page that exists only as an open sketch;
the flow then shows its first variant. Lines hold for every preset. Without `position`, Studio
lays the frames out along the lines.

### Draw a wireframe

A wireframe exists to iterate fast, in minutes per round, rough enough to redraw with a client at
the table. It answers one thing: which regions a screen has and what each region holds. These
rules are strict:

- **Keep what exists.** Before a sketch, list what the running app already does on that screen.
  Keep it as a labelled box, and draw only what is still open.
- **One sketch per screen or flow**, never one per region or per detail. The variants differ in
  layout: where the regions sit and how big they are.
- **Regions and names only.** A region is a box with a label; a list shows item names. Draw no
  counts, badges, status markers, inspectors, size labels or field lists. If a detail matters,
  write it as a word in the region label.
- **Never polish.** Do not fix alignment, spacing or a kit gap. When the kit lacks a shape, draw a
  labelled box. Look at each shot only for a broken frame: overflow, a scroll bar, clipped text.
- **Draw it yourself.** A wireframe round is small work: no subagent, no friction report.
- **Stop early.** When the regions of the main screens are settled, the stage ends. Comments on
  the look of a wireframe belong to the next stage, not to a new wireframe round.

A page may not import another page. To show a page inside a page ("in context"), embed it:
`embedPage('pages/system', { state, width, height, scale })` from `@design-system` answers a
drawing whose `body` is a frame of that page, drawn in the same product, sketch variant and theme
as the embedding frame. `width` and `height` are the viewport the page is drawn at (default
1280 x 800; `height: 'auto'` fits its content), `scale` shrinks the frame. Never rebuild a page
from its elements to show it.

A page that has no parts yet draws grey stand-ins from the wireframe kit; pages and elements may
import it, components and foundations may not:

```ts
import { box, heading, textLines, image, button, input, icon, select } from '@design-system/kit';
```

Signatures are in `libs/cli/design/wireframe-kit.ts`: `box(children, { direction, gap, padding, width, height, grow, plain, stackBelow, fill })`,
`heading(text, { size })`, `textLines({ lines, width, size })`, `image({ width, height, ratio })`,
`button(label, { primary })`, `input({ label, placeholder, width })`, `icon({ size, glyph })`,
`select({ label, value, width })`, `tabs(labels, { active })`, `segmented(options, { active })`,
`checkbox(label, { checked })`, `badge(text)` and `dot({ hollow, size })`. Draw a control as its
type: a picker is a `select`, a section switch `tabs`, a size switch `segmented`, a count a `badge`,
a status a `dot`, never a row of buttons or an empty `icon`. Give an icon a `glyph` (`'plus'`,
`'close'`, `'menu'`, `'more'`, …; another name draws its first letter). Give the root box of a page or a
shell `fill: true` so it is as tall as the frame, instead of a hand-written `min-height`. Draw for
every preset, not one width: give a picture a `ratio` (`'2/3'`) instead of a fixed height, and give
a row `stackBelow: <px>`, the width below which it stacks its children, instead of fixed widths
that only fit the desktop. Never use `vh`, `dvh` or `svh` in a part: a part has no viewport of its own, so the unit measures Studio's frame, not the page. A full page is a frame of a fixed size. Put titles in `heading`, never in hand-written markup. Studio lists such a page under
"Wireframes" with its kit-use count. A shell is a normal element named by purpose (`shell-main`); draw a rough one with the kit, so each
page imports the shell instead of repeating it, and a shell pick lands in one file.
A dialog without its own URL is an element that a page state shows ("login open"). Examples in
`.ethlete/design/studio-lab`: `pages/film-detail`, `elements/shell-main`, `elements/login-dialog`,
`flows/sign-in.json`.

### Check a product

```bash
et design check --product <name>   # layer dependencies, hard-coded colours, undefined tokens, copied components, scripted motion, tsc, render
et design system --json            # each part's origin, note, states, presets and problems
```

Without `--product`, `check` covers every product. A part may only use its own layer and the
layers below it (see "The order of a design"). Rule `FLOW` reports a misshaped flow file, a frame
naming a part or state that exists neither in the product nor in an open sketch of that part, a duplicate state, and a line to a state that is not a frame of
the flow. Rule `WIREFRAME-KIT` reports a component or foundation importing the kit. Pass the changed files to the check below as before.

Once the other rules pass, the check draws every state in a headless Chromium on a server of its own
(pages at each preset, a part with `widths` at each width, any other part fitted), and
`sketch check` does the same for the open variants and the pages they show in. Each line names
product, part, state, size and a selector path:

- `OVERFLOW` - the frame scrolls: content wider than the frame, or taller than a preset height.
- `CLIPPED` - an element with `overflow: hidden|clip` cuts its content, unless it sets
  `text-overflow: ellipsis` or a line clamp.
- `WRAP` - text in a button, tab, badge, chip or `white-space: nowrap` box runs onto a second line.
- `ZERO-SIZE` - the part root has no width or no height.
- `UNKNOWN-THEME` - a `et-color--<name>` class names a colour theme no stylesheet of the frame defines, so it draws in the fallback colour.
- `RENDER` - the frame refused to draw, or the part did not load.

A part that breaks a rule on purpose names it: `definePart({ checks: { skip: ['CLIPPED'] }, … })`;
the skip covers the part wherever it is drawn. Without Playwright Chromium the check prints
`RENDER CHECK SKIPPED` and passes on the other rules.

A project's `config.json` entry can name `themes`, `{ "surface": [...], "color": [...] }`; a
frame asked for a theme gets the `et-surface--<name>` and `et-color--<name>` classes on its root,
so a drawing must take its colours from the theme tokens and never set a surface or colour class
on its own root. An inner panel may set `et-surface--<name>`.

`et design [checkout]` serves the frames; the checkout defaults to the working directory and
`DE_PORT` overrules the port. In the ethlete SDK the user reads Studio, started with `yarn studio`,
which serves the frames itself: do not start `yarn design` next to it. Studio carries its own copy
of the tool, so a checkout that installs nothing still draws.

Three constraints on a drawing file:

- **Never import a package barrel.** The libraries resolve to source, so one barrel makes the
  browser request every module and the requests fail with `ERR_INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES`. Import
  the one file you need.
- **The fixture is shared, and a variant may not change it.**
- **One file per variant**, so a broken variant breaks its own frame only.

A `<script>` in a drawing never runs. For behavior give the drawing a `setup(root)` function
(called once after the markup is in `root`, no cleanup, wire one delegated listener). Render each
state of a prototype with `ngStates({ closed: …, open: … }, { imports })` and swap them with
`setup: flow.on([{ click: '.trigger', go: 'open' }])`. To draw an open overlay, open it in the
template (`<et-select [open]="true">`); `ng()` returns the real panel and the frame places it.
`ngStates` wraps the states in `<div data-de-states style="display: contents">`, so a selector
rule must not depend on that wrapper.

**A repository with a sketch Storybook** draws every variant in the **same** story, side by
side, under the real geometry the thing ships in. The default Storybook is
http://localhost:4400; an app with its own sketch Storybook names its port in the plan file.

Either way:

- Sketches take inputs only and stay out of the application's build.
- Prototype, never refactor. Do not touch the shipped component until the treatment is
  settled.
- Keep the rejected variants drawn, marked as rejected.

### Notes

A note explains a state: why it looks this way, what it shows. A comment is feedback that needs
an answer. Write a note when nothing is asked of the reader.

A note is `<product>/notes/<timestamp>-<id>.json`:

```json
{ "part": "button", "state": "disabled", "point": { "x": 24, "y": 8 }, "size": "mobile", "text": "Muted, not hidden." }
```

- `part`, `state` and `text` are required. `point` is optional, in CSS pixels.
- `size` is required when `point` is set: the preset, the CSS pixel width, or `"fitted"` the note was written at. A
  pointed note shows only at that size; a note without a point shows at every size.
- A free note on a flow is an entry in the `notes` array of `flows/<name>.json`:
  `{ "id": "…", "text": "…", "at": { "x": 0, "y": -40 } }`. `at` is optional, the note's top-left
  corner on the flow canvas, and may be negative.

## The order of a design

A product design runs in this order. Each stage settles in calls before the next starts, and
each stage draws with what the stages before it settled (the wireframes draw with the kit only):

1. **Wireframes**: early, rough concepts of the main flows (a legacy call with `mode: 'wireframe'`;
   in a product, draw them with the wireframe kit, see "Draw a wireframe"). They show
   which components the product needs, not how they look. The stage ends with an inventory in
   the wireframe call: every part the wireframes need, each mapped to the SDK component it
   starts from, or marked new with the component call that draws it. The inventory is the
   queue of component calls:

   ```ts
   inventory: [
     { part: 'Search field', sdk: 'et-input' },
     { part: 'Match card', new: true, call: 'tomflix/components/match-card' },
   ],
   ```

2. **Foundations**: colours, colour themes and surface themes (the project's `themes` in
   `config.json`), plus the type scale, spacing and radius.
3. **Logo and CI**, if the project needs them.
4. **Components**, the inventory is their queue, from the SDK ones rendered with `ng()`, themed and set up for the project.
   Each accepted one becomes a design-system entry.
5. **Larger elements**: the shell, the navigation, headers, lists, built from the entries.
6. **Pages**, built from the elements and the entries.
7. **The working prototype**: the pages joined with `ngStates` and `flow.on`.

Do not start a stage before the one above it is settled, and do not draw a page from parts that
are not in the design system. If the user asks for a later stage first, say which earlier stage
is missing, and draw that first.

The stages map onto the layers of a product: wireframes, foundations, components, elements, pages. A settled
Legacy call with a stage counts for that stage in this order.

A later stage can show that an earlier one is incomplete. If a page needs a part that the system
does not have, add it to the inventory. A part becomes a component only when at least two hosts
draw the same case. Until then it stays in the one element or page that draws it. When a second
host draws it, open a component sketch, and list in its brief every host and every case each one
draws, so the component covers them all.

A component documents its states per axis, not every combination: for example kind, end mark and
interaction (rest, hover, focus-visible, selected, inert), plus only the combinations that look
different. A smaller piece with no states of its own, such as an icon set, is a foundation asset,
not a component.

## Draw from the design system

A call that invents its own button, field or row does not match the calls beside it. **Before
you draw a part, look for it in this order, and draw new only when none of them has it:**

1. The product's design system, `.ethlete/design/<product>/` (and its base).
2. The real SDK components, rendered on the design server with `ng()` from `@design-explore`:

   ```ts
   const field = await ng(`<et-form-field><et-label>Name</et-label><et-input /></et-form-field>`, {
     imports: ['FORM_FIELD_IMPORTS', 'INPUT_IMPORTS'],
   });
   ```

   The template is a real Angular template, and `imports` names exports of
   `@ethlete/components`. The project's `providers` module in `config.json` supplies the themes.
   Render every component of a drawing in **one** `ng()` call: each call is a new app, so two
   calls repeat element ids. The server renders the built package, so in the SDK rebuild
   `dist` after a component change.

   To draw a form state (a value, an error, a touched field), give `ng()` (or `ngStates()`)
   `fields`. Each entry becomes a signal form field the template binds as
   `[formField]="fields.<name>"`. An error is a kind (`'required'`) or a kind and a message. A
   field shows its errors only when it is touched:

   ```ts
   const form = await ng(
     `<et-form-field><et-label>Email</et-label><et-input [formField]="fields.email" /></et-form-field>`,
     {
       imports: ['FORM_FIELD_IMPORTS', 'INPUT_IMPORTS'],
       fields: { email: { value: 'ada@', errors: [{ kind: 'email', message: 'Not an email' }], touched: true } },
     },
   );
   ```

3. Only then a new drawing. Build it from the two above, and say in the variant's `claim`
   that the part is new.

A part is one folder, `<product>/<layer>/<part>/`, with its drawing and states. Read the parts of
the product before the first drawing of a session. **A part exists only because the user picked a
sketch.** A `chosen` verdict in an old call is not enough. Never change a part's look without a
sketch the user decided.

## Check before you look

A broken build draws an overlay, so a screenshot of it looks like a design. **One check
covers that, and it is the whole gate.** Name the files you changed, never a whole project,
which is far slower and can fight the user's own editor.

With `et design`, run the checker from the checkout it draws:

```bash
et design check --lint <changed files> --tsconfig
```

`--tsconfig` with no path types every call of the checkout. `--tsconfig` also types each variant of
an open sketch and prints the tsc output of a failing one. `--checkout <path>` names another
one.

With a Storybook, copy `check-story.mjs` (bundled next to this skill) to the **repository root** first:

```bash
node check-story.mjs --lint <changed files> --tsconfig apps/<app>/.storybook/tsconfig.json
```

Both take about four seconds and need no dev server. Then stop and hand the slug to the
user. Do not also render it in a browser: it costs a browser launch, and both tools
transpile without type checking, so the render reports `ok` on a file that does not
compile. Open it only when the check passes and the drawing still does not appear:

```bash
et design check --call <slug>             # every variant of the call
et design check --call <slug> --variant b # one of them
node check-story.mjs --tsconfig <path> --story <story-id>
```

## Delegating a sketch

Every brief names `model: opus`, and every prompt names the exact model id the sub-agent runs on,
for example "Your model id is `claude-opus-5-5`; pass `--by claude-opus-5-5` to every write
command." You know the id because you chose the model; the sub-agent does not, and must not guess.

1. **One agent per sketch.** It draws all the variants of the sketch. Give it the sketch folder, the
   fixture it must not change, and the claim of each variant. Do not spawn one agent per
   variant: each would re-read the skill, the call, the fixture and the example, about 45-57k
   tokens each, so the cost is several times higher. Calls are independent, so several calls
   can run at once, one agent each.
2. **One check-and-fix agent, after the drawing agents return.** Give it the changed files
   and the call slug. It runs the check above, fixes what it reports, and repeats until the
   check says `ok`. It may not change what a variant draws, only what stops it rendering.
3. **One write-up agent, once the user settles the sketch in Studio.** Give it the verdict in the
   user's own words and the plan file. It records what won, what lost and why, it sets each
   variant's `verdict` in an old call's `call.ts` (a product sketch needs none; the merge sets the note). It runs while you open
   the next call.

## Screenshots

**Off by default.** The user has the call open and sends you a picture when something looks
wrong. Take one only when the code cannot tell you whether two variants really differ, and
never to put in front of the user. Copy `shoot-template.mjs` (bundled next to this skill) to the repository
root.

```bash
node shoot.mjs <story-id> 1100 760 out.png
```

- `waitUntil: 'networkidle'` never settles on an iframe that holds a live dev server
  connection. Use `'domcontentloaded'`.
- `:hover`, `:focus-visible` and `:active` need a CDP session and `CSS.forcePseudoState`.
  Several hold open at once, so one image shows them all. The template does this.

## Writing it down

Every settled call goes in the exploration's plan file: what won, what lost, and why. Keep
an **Open** list for the calls not yet made. A rejected variant written down stops the next
session from drawing it again. After a clear rejection, use that record to frame and draw the
next call; do not wait for the user to type “continue”.
